name: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate
lead: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate (MAP) is a water-soluble derivative of vitamin C used as an ingredient in skincare products, where it is marketed as a more stable alternative to L-ascorbic acid. It is described in the literature as a pro-drug of vitamin C, meaning it is meant to be converted to ascorbic acid after reaching the skin. [3]

Laboratory work has found that ascorbic acid and its derivatives are more stable as ascorbyl esters than as the free acid in solution and in topical formulations. [4] A cosmetic ingredient safety review covering ascorbic acid and several of its salts and phosphate esters, including MAP, was published in the International Journal of Toxicology in 2005. [6]

Evidence for MAP specifically on appearance outcomes is limited. One small formulation study reported improved skin hydration with a MAP product, while a broader review of topical vitamin C notes that clinical studies of topical formulations are limited and that stability and penetration are the main challenges. [7][5]

paras: MAP appears in serums, creams and masks marketed for brightening, antioxidant protection and anti-aging. Reviews of topical vitamin C describe antioxidant, photoprotective, collagen-related and pigment-reducing effects for the vitamin as a class, though these reviews note that clinical data on formulated topical products are limited. [5]

L-ascorbic acid is unstable in solution, which motivated the development of derivatives. A 1997 analytical study found that ascorbyl palmitate and MAP were more stable than ascorbic acid in standard solutions and topical formulations. [4]

Percutaneous absorption research on pig skin examined ascorbic acid and its derivatives to define formulation features that deliver vitamin C into skin. [2] An in vitro study found that lasers and microdermabrasion increased skin permeation of vitamin C and also examined MAP delivery. [3] A 2019 study reported that hyaluronic acid microneedles were fabricated to enhance MAP delivery into skin. [10]

A Cosmetic Ingredient Review-style safety assessment of ascorbic acid, its calcium, magnesium and sodium salts, and magnesium and sodium ascorbyl phosphate, as used in cosmetics, was published in 2005. [6] Individual products carry their own label warnings, for example external use only and avoiding eye contact.

Published human data on MAP are sparse. A study comparing ascorbic acid, MAP and ascorbyl tetra-isopalmitate applied to forearm skin for four weeks in volunteers reported that all formulations increased stratum corneum hydration; only the ascorbic acid product changed transepidermal water loss, and the MAP product changed a skin elasticity ratio. The authors concluded MAP improved hydration while derivatives did not match ascorbic acid on water loss. In laboratory antioxidant tests in the same study, ascorbic acid was strongest in the water-based system. [7]
Registered clinical trials listing MAP are dental gel studies for periodontitis and peri-implantitis rather than cosmetic studies. [11][12]

card.summary: A stable, water-soluble vitamin C derivative in brightening serums; common in products, thin on direct human trials.
card.note: Human data specific to MAP are sparse; most vitamin C evidence concerns L-ascorbic acid.

quick.overview:
Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate is a vitamin C derivative used in cosmetic serums and creams. It is promoted as being more stable than pure ascorbic acid.

Published evidence for its appearance effects is limited; one small study reported improved skin hydration, and reviews say clinical data on topical vitamin C are limited overall.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a pro-drug that is converted to ascorbic acid in skin. Laboratory studies show it is more stable than ascorbic acid in formulations, while penetration into skin is the main challenge discussed in the literature.
quick.risks: A cosmetic safety assessment covering MAP was published in 2005. It is a cosmetic ingredient sold without prescription; product labels advise external use and avoiding the eyes.
